classification_signals: Abstract states 'This paper deals with and asks...' and summarizes findings from various fields (p. 2).

Background section explicitly states 'This report provides the theoretical basis for this semester's parallel design work. Different disciplines were brought together, from the fields of architectural history, architectural theory, natural sciences and psychology.' (p. 4).
Methodology section states 'The focus in the preparation of this report was on literature studies from various disciplines and research of studies.' (p. 4).
The paper extensively cites other research throughout, synthesizing findings to support its theoretical propositions and design proposal (e.g., pages 6, 9, 11-14).
The 'Proposal' section (p. 18-20) outlines a design concept based on the literature review, rather than presenting empirical results from the author's own study.

The 'Conclusion' section (p. 22) discusses the limitations of the *cited* evidence and the applicability of the *project* (design proposal), not limitations of an empirical study conducted by the author.

limitations: The project is limited to the domestic space for a single person.
The project is not applicable to the living conditions of people with physical disabilities.
The project does not provide suitable conditions for families and other forms of community living.

A large part of the evidence used on the effects on mental health or social behavior comes from studies with an environment optimized for the study and therefore does not correspond to real conditions of daily life.
The applicability of findings in reality cannot be determined with certainty and must be investigated by further studies under real-life conditions.
Effects of temperature on other senses (e.g., thermal conditions on acoustic or olfactory stimuli) were not considered.
minimum_safe_summary: This paper, 'Of Sweating and Freezing: Temperature as design factor in architecture,' serves as a theoretical report exploring temperature as a crucial, often overlooked, design factor in architecture. It synthesizes literature from architectural history, theory, natural sciences, and psychology to argue that indoor climate is more than just comfort, significantly impacting human health, cognitive abilities, and social behavior. Key findings highlight that a single ideal temperature does not exist, as individual differences (like gender and age) influence thermal needs, and inappropriate temperatures can lead to chronic stress and mental/physical illness. Conversely, warmth fosters social attachment and generosity, while cold can protect mental health. The paper proposes a design approach where architectural form and function follow temperature, creating varied thermal zones through core heat sources, natural air circulation, and material effusivity to enhance well-being and social interaction. Limitations include the project's focus on single-person domestic spaces, its inapplicability to individuals with physical disabilities or communal living, and the reliance on evidence from optimized study environments rather than real-life conditions, suggesting a need for further empirical research on temperature's cross-modal effects.
